title: Removal Costs Plus $75 Million: the Cap Written in 1990 and the Blowout the Commission Called Preventable
participants: Minerals Management Service / Department of the Interior
National Commission on the BP Deepwater Horizon Oil Spill and Offshore Drilling
Congress of the United States (Oil Pollution Act 1990)

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The saving was in time and procedure at the end of a well that was late and over budget, and the Commission locates it precisely: "BP's management process did not adequately identify or address risks created by late changes to well design and procedures", and BP "did not have adequate controls in place to ensure that key decisions in the months leading up to the blowout were safe or sound from an engineering perspective." Initial well design went through peer review; the changes made in the weeks and days before did not go through the same process.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The Commission declines to treat the failure as one firm's: the immediate causes "can be traced to a series of identifiable mistakes made by BP, Halliburton, and Transocean that reveal such systematic failures in risk management that they place in doubt the safety culture of the entire industry." And on the other side of the relationship, it finds "failures of government to provide effective regulatory oversight of offshore drilling."
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog here is the one the Commission spends its root-cause chapter dispelling: the account of the blowout as an accident of the frontier, a statistical inevitability of deep water. "The blowout was not the product of a series of aberrational decisions made by rogue industry or government officials that could not have been anticipated or expected to occur again. Rather, the root causes are systemic and, absent significant reform in both industry practices and government policies, might well recur." And: "A blowout in deepwater was not a statistical inevitability."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall is the cap, and it was written twenty years earlier. Under the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, the total liability of a responsible party for an offshore facility is limited to "the total of all removal costs plus $75,000,000" — a figure fixed in 1990 and never indexed, against a well whose eventual costs ran to many billions. The limit does not apply where the incident was proximately caused by gross negligence, wilful misconduct or a regulatory violation, and whether it would have held at Macondo was never adjudicated. It did not need to be: a cap this far below the exposure shapes what is risked before anything goes wrong.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The Commission is the Mersey step in its benign form, and it says what such bodies usually do not. Its first conclusion is that "The explosive loss of the Macondo well could have been prevented", and its root-cause chapter refuses the exculpatory reading in advance: "Whatever irreducible uncertainty may persist regarding the precise contribution to the blowout of each of several potentially immediate causes, no such uncertainty exists about the blowout's root causes." It was nonetheless advisory. It determined no liability, brought no proceedings, and its recommendations bound no one.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The statutory liability limit, the instrument this atlas first meets in the 1851 Limitation of Liability Act and the 1914 Titanic judgment, rewritten for oil in 1990 as a removal-costs-plus-$75,000,000 ceiling on an offshore facility.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-Macondo reorganisation of offshore regulation — the splitting of the agency that had both collected royalties from drilling and policed its safety — and a standing recommendation set that the Commission itself noted would bind nobody.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The cap sets the maximum downside of a deepwater well; the upside is uncapped; the regulator that might have adjusted the balance was funded from the activity it policed. The Commission's finding that the root causes "might well recur" is a statement about that arithmetic, not about any particular crew.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Macondo was the price of the frontier — an unforeseeable accident in water too deep and pressures too high for anyone to have managed — or, the mirror image, that one company's uniquely reckless culture explains all of it.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The Commission rejected both in the same paragraph. Against the frontier account: "The explosive loss of the Macondo well could have been prevented", and "A blowout in deepwater was not a statistical inevitability." Against the single-bad-actor account: the mistakes were "made by BP, Halliburton, and Transocean" and reveal "systematic failures in risk management that they place in doubt the safety culture of the entire industry", with root causes that "are systemic" and extend to "failures of government to provide effective regulatory oversight". What the Commission did not do is assign liability — it was advisory, and said so.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A statutory liability ceiling for an offshore facility of removal costs plus $75,000,000, enacted in 1990 and unindexed, subject to exceptions for gross negligence, wilful misconduct and regulatory violation that were never adjudicated here. A presidential commission finding that the loss "could have been prevented"; that its immediate causes trace to identifiable mistakes by three named companies; that those mistakes reveal systematic risk-management failures placing the whole industry's safety culture in doubt; that most of them trace back to "a single overarching failure — a failure of management"; that BP's process did not address the risks created by late changes to well design and procedures; and that the root causes are systemic and, without reform in both industry practice and government policy, "might well recur".

citations.title: National Commission on the BP Deepwater Horizon Oil Spill and Offshore Drilling, Deep Water: The Gulf Oil Disaster and the Future of Offshore Drilling — Report to the President (January 2011)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from govinfo and read as extracted text. The Commission's own conclusions, stated as a list: "The explosive loss of the Macondo well could have been prevented." "The immediate causes of the Macondo well blowout can be traced to a series of identifiable mistakes made by BP, Halliburton, and Transocean that reveal such systematic failures in risk management that they place in doubt the safety culture of the entire industry." "Deepwater energy exploration and production, particularly at the frontiers of experience, involve risks for which neither industry nor government has been adequately prepared". On root causes: "Whatever irreducible uncertainty may persist regarding the precise contribution to the blowout of each of several potentially immediate causes, no such uncertainty exists about the blowout's root causes. The blowout was not the product of a series of aberrational decisions made by rogue industry or government officials that could not have been anticipated or expected to occur again. Rather, the root causes are systemic and, absent significant reform in both industry practices and government policies, might well recur. The missteps were rooted in systemic failures by industry management (extending beyond BP to contractors that serve many in the industry), and also by failures of government to provide effective regulatory oversight of offshore drilling." And: "most of the mistakes and oversights at Macondo can be traced back to a single overarching failure--a failure of management ... A blowout in deepwater was not a statistical inevitability." The Commission also records that "BP's management process did not adequately identify or address risks created by late changes to well design and procedures" and that BP "did not have adequate controls in place to ensure that key decisions in the months leading up to the blowout were safe or sound from an engineering perspective." The Commission was advisory; it determined no liability and brought no proceedings.

citations.title: Oil Pollution Act of 1990, section 1004, codified at 33 U.S.C. § 2704 — Limits on liability (U.S. Code, 2011 edition)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from govinfo and read as extracted text. The general rule caps a responsible party's total liability for removal costs and damages per incident, and subsection (a)(3) sets the figure that governed an offshore facility in 2010: "(3) for an offshore facility except a deepwater port, the total of all removal costs plus $75,000,000; and (4) for any onshore facility and a deepwater port, $350,000,000." Subsection (b) provides that a mobile offshore drilling unit used as an offshore facility is "deemed to be a tank vessel" first, and is "deemed to be an offshore facility" for liability in excess of the tank-vessel amount. A TEXT CAUTION WORTH RECORDING: the Statutes at Large scan of the same provision (STATUTE-104-Pg484) is an image whose OCR renders paragraph (3) as "for a n onshore facility", dropping the "ff" — which inverts the meaning, since onshore facilities are paragraph (4). The United States Code text above is the one read and cited here; the Statutes at Large scan was opened, found corrupt at this point, and is not cited. The cap does not apply where the incident was proximately caused by gross negligence, wilful misconduct, or violation of an applicable regulation (33 U.S.C. § 2704(c)); whether it would have applied to Macondo was never adjudicated, and nothing here asserts that it limited what was ultimately paid.
